# THEORYs with `tags` `self`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Self** — what a self is — the minimal, bodily and pre-reflective self, self-models and the sense of being a subject, the self as process or as context, and whether machines or groups can be selves. Not the person, which is personhood (group: philosophy; ADR-024).

| [THEORY-044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-044.md) v2 | In relational frame theory the self is verbal behaviour's content, its process and its context, and the self as context is a perspective learned from deictic relations that cannot itself be found as content | Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) define three selves: the conceptualized self, the content of verbal relations about oneself; the knowing self, their ongoing process; and the transcendent self, their context. Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) say the third arises from deictic frames (I–you, here–there, now–then) as "a sense of self as a locus or perspective", and is "a context for verbal knowing, not the content", so its limits "cannot be consciously known". The account maps the three onto the record's holdings: the content is the narrative self (Dennett, Gallagher, Strawson), and the context is what Hume could not find among his perceptions and what Metzinger calls a transparent perspective. It differs from the minimal self (Gallagher) on origin: RFT says the perspective is learned in language. The evidence for the learned origin is cited, not read, so Proposed. The clinical claim is [THEORY-051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-051.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-051.md) v4 | Strengthening the self as context, a perspective from which thoughts about oneself are held as thoughts, is a process by which acceptance and commitment therapy reduces suffering | ACT names the self as context as one of its six processes: from it "one can be aware of ones own flow of experiences without attachment to them", so it fosters defusion and acceptance, and mindfulness exercises and metaphors foster it (Hayes et al., [LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)). RFT reads defusion as moving thoughts from I HERE NOW to I THERE THEN, a deictic shift (Barnes-Holmes et al., [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)), labelled "no more than a heuristic". No study in the record tests the self as context as a process. Its only support is borrowed from small defusion studies under RFT's reading, so Proposed on weak grounds. The conceptual account of the self is [THEORY-044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-044.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-054](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-054.md) v3 | A regulation is autonomous to the degree it is integrated with one's other values and needs: autonomy is graded, and is not set by the order of the attitude that endorses it | Self-determination theory orders motives on a continuum from external through introjected and identified to integrated regulation and intrinsic motivation. Ryan and Deci ([LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md)) and Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)) place autonomy in integration, "congruence with one's other values and needs", and report a quasi-simplex structure and an experiment in which integrated and introjected internalization behave differently. It is not shown that integration can be measured apart from endorsement, and it does not escape Velleman's dilemma. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-063](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-063.md) | The unity of experience is the integration of one global world-model into a single functional cluster, and it does not require a self-model | Metzinger's précis of Being No One (2005), [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md): the globality constraint makes every conscious content part of one world-model. On the functional level that is "highest-order binding" into a single causal role, and on the neural level the prediction of "one single area of maximal causal density", after Tononi and Edelman's dynamic core. "What you subjectively experience upon experiencing your world as coherent is the high internal correlation strength between a subset of physical events in your own brain." The neural half is a cited hypothesis, the précis says little is known, and how the cluster becomes one subject's is left open. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-064](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-064.md) | What is experienced as a self is the content of a self-model the system cannot recognise as a model, and nothing beyond such models is a self | Metzinger's précis of Being No One (2005), [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md), with his encyclopedia article "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md)): a phenomenal self is a transparent self-model, one whose representational character "is not accessible to subjective experience", so that the system experiences its content "simply as ourselves". Selfhood is "a function realized by a lack of information", and "no such things as selves exist in the world". | [THEORY-074](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-074.md) | Implicit accessibility of the true self-concept is not what self-report scales of authenticity or of need satisfaction measure, though those two self-reports are not shown to be separate constructs | Schlegel, Hicks, Arndt & King (2009), [LIT-606](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-606.md): true-self accessibility, the speed of "me" judgments for traits a person takes to be her true self, correlated .05 with AI-3 authenticity and .20 with basic need satisfaction (N = 124), and each predicted meaning in life independently. | [THEORY-093](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-093.md) v2 | A content of mind is conscious when a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings identifies it as the organism's own; the feelings are conscious in themselves and hybrid, partly made of the body state they map, because interoceptive pathways let the body act directly on the neurons that map it | Damasio & Damasio (2022), [LIT-628](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-628.md), an essay with no data, read only through a summarising fetch tool, so its wording is paraphrased here. Consciousness is the spontaneous identification of mind contents as belonging to one's own organism, and a continuous stream of homeostatic feelings, from hunger and pain to a faint feeling of existing, supplies it; the feelings are conscious in themselves and confer consciousness on exteroceptive images. They are hybrid because interoceptive axons are unmyelinated, partly non-synaptic and outside a systematic blood–brain barrier, so viscera and circulating molecules act on the neurons that map them. Damasio & Carvalho (2013), [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md), read in full, supply the upper-brainstem site of feeling and the unmyelinated-fibre proposal. Proposed: the identification is a definition, the mechanism an interpretation of anatomy, and the clinical evidence does not separate this account from its rivals. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-147](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-147.md) | Deep responsibility is not limited to the moral, and attributability and accountability are independent kinds of it rather than two levels: accountability needs only that the agent acted as she ought not to, was in a position to know it, and that acting so was up to her, while what makes a self a fit target of the reactive attitudes is plausibly that it can perceive, understand and appreciate the world as we do | Wolf (2015), [LIT-747](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-747.md), the 2013 Routledge Lecture. We are deeply, not merely causally, responsible for nonmoral traits and art, by the self-disclosure view. Watson's two-level view, accountability as attributability plus control, is rejected: a stipulated psychopath may be accountable for acts whose source is not attributable to him. Fitness for reactive attitudes is, on Wolf's hunch, being an intelligent self. Proposed: the positive view is her hunch. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-406](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-406.md) v2 | Self-presentations that differ by audience coexist without trouble while the audiences are kept apart by spatial, social and temporal boundaries, and collide when a medium removes the boundaries; networked publics make the collision frequent and often unseen by the person it happens to | boyd (2008), [LIT-1001](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1001.md), after Meyrowitz (1985), read in part: §1.5, §4.4, the Top Friends passage and every passage on context, segmentation, collision and Goffman in [NOTE-710](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-710.md), and Chapters 1, 4 and 7 in full in [NOTE-1432](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1432.md) (both Skimmed). | [THEORY-409](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-409.md) | A person's mind is normally a system of parts that take protective roles, managers, exiles and firefighters, forced on them by experience and not part of their nature; beneath the parts is a Self, distinct from all of them and present from the start, which appears with calm, curiosity and compassion when the parts step back and which heals by leading the system | Schwartz, [LIT-579](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-579.md) (the IFS Institute's "Evolution" essay, read in [NOTE-453](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-453.md)) and [LIT-591](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-591.md) (Internal Family Systems Therapy, chapter 1 only, [NOTE-457](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-457.md), Skimmed). | [THEORY-458](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-458.md) v2 | Within the minimal self, the sense that a movement or a thought is mine and the sense that I am its source are distinct and come apart, as in involuntary movement and thought insertion; on Frith's comparator model the sense of agency depends on a forward model that precedes action and ownership on sensory feedback, so failed forward monitoring would explain thought insertion and, by the same mechanism, why first-person reference ordinarily cannot misidentify its subject | Gallagher (2000), [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md), read in [NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md) from the preprint. It does not say which minimal self, embodied or reflective, the analysis concerns. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-490](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-490.md) v2 | What a chat agent's 'I' refers to is fixed by the context of use, not by the system: the agent role-plays characters that carry the self-conception the corpus and the conversation give them, and its uses of 'I' can pick out the model, present in many simultaneous instances, or the single conversation, none of them the self by nature | Shanahan (2025), [LIT-466](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-466.md), read in [NOTE-376](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-376.md), with Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds (2023), [LIT-460](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-460.md), read for the self in [NOTE-370](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-370.md). | [THEORY-590](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-590.md) | The self whose governance makes action autonomous is not the self whose persistence is personal identity: governance by an essence of volitional necessities would make action authentic, not autonomous; losing a defining care costs one's grasp of who one is, not one's existence; and wholeheartedness won by extruding a desire is a defence, not health | Velleman (2002), [LIT-292](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-292.md), read in [NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md). A critique of Frankfurt's late (1990s) view that autonomy is governance by the essential character of the will, an essence that is also the condition of one's identity. It argues by counterexample (Winnicott's False Self, the Agamemnon sequel), from Freud's Rat Man, and by debunking genealogy. The positive view, that "self" marks reflexivity and that autonomous action is motivated in part by the understanding, is stated "briefly" and argued elsewhere. Frankfurt's reply is unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-650](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-650.md) | Whether a self at one time is the same as a self at another has an answer only relative to a level of abstraction fixed by the purpose of asking, and asked at no such level it has none; the question with a substantive answer is what makes a self one thing at a time | Floridi (2011), [LIT-136](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-136.md), read in [NOTE-130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-130.md). | [THEORY-681](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-681.md) | If every real idea derives from an impression, there is no idea of a simple self persisting through life; the mind is a bundle of perceptions, and the identity ascribed to it is produced by the imagination passing easily along resemblance and causation, as with a rebuilt ship or a growing oak, though Hume's Appendix concedes that this does not explain what unites the perceptions | Hume (1739, with the Appendix of 1740), [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md), read in [NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md). | [THEORY-684](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-684.md) | Experiencing oneself as a self that was there in the further past, seeking pattern in one's life, fitting it to a story and falsifying it in the telling are separable, and fitting it to a story suffices for narrativity; on testimony that some normal people are Episodic and live good lives, neither the claim that people experience their lives as narratives nor the claim that a good life or full personhood needs it holds in general | Strawson (2004), [LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md), read in [NOTE-383](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-383.md). | [THEORY-691](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-691.md) | A self is an abstractum like a centre of gravity, posited by interpreting a person's behaviour and talk, the brain's own autobiography included; it is as determinate as that story, it can be authored by a process with no self in it, and a body holds as many selves as the points the best story coheres around | Dennett (1992), [LIT-442](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-442.md), read in [NOTE-364](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-364.md) from a copy-edited transcription. | [THEORY-765](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-765.md) v2 | Brushing a seen rubber hand in synchrony with the hidden real hand makes touch be felt at the rubber hand, makes it be reported as one's own, and shifts the felt position of the real hand toward it; a small asynchrony removes these effects | Botvinick & Cohen (1998), [LIT-1277](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1277.md), read in full in [NOTE-1006](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1006.md). Its suggestion control was also too weak to separate perception from expectation (Lush & Seth 2022, LIT-1267). The report half is restated, narrower, in THEORY-766. |
| [THEORY-766](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-766.md) v2 | Brushing a seen rubber hand in synchrony with the hidden real hand, against asynchronous brushing, raises reports that touch is felt at the rubber hand and, more weakly and less reliably, that the rubber hand is one's own; the proprioceptive drift toward the rubber hand that accompanies these reports is not a measure of them; the standard comparison conditions do not equalise participants' expectations, so whether the stimulation or the expectation produces the report difference is open | Botvinick & Cohen (1998) and four replications read here give a synchrony effect on reports of referred touch and ownership. Rohde et al. (2011) and Abdulkarim & Ehrsson (2016) separate drift from ownership. The suggestion debate (Lush 2020; Lush et al. 2020; Ehrsson et al. 2022; Lush & Seth 2022; Roseboom & Lush 2022) shows that the standard controls do not equalise expectations. The ownership report is weaker than the referred-touch report and tracks trait suggestibility. Whether the synchronous stimulation, not expectation, produces the report difference is not settled. Promoted 2026-10-20 on the report differences measured ([ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v3); the perceptual reading is [THEORY-827](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-827.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-767](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-767.md) v2 | Body ownership draws on interoceptive as well as exteroceptive signals: a visual cue synchronous with one's heartbeat increases ownership of a virtual hand and identification with a virtual body, and lower interoceptive sensitivity goes with greater susceptibility to the rubber hand illusion | Seth (2013), [LIT-1263](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1263.md), read in full in [NOTE-1000](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1000.md). An opinion article that reports, at second hand, that a virtual hand pulsing with the heartbeat was owned more (Suzuki et al. 2013, the author's own group), that a virtual body pulsing with it was identified with more (Aspell et al. 2013), and that people with lower heartbeat-detection sensitivity are more susceptible to the rubber hand illusion (Tsakiris et al. 2011). None of the studies was read here, and no control separates the heartbeat from any other periodic signal. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-768](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-768.md) v2 | Minimal selfhood is identification with the whole body, located where that body is felt to be and seen from inside it; owning a body part does not reach it, and bodily agency enables it causally without being part of it | Blanke & Metzinger (2009), [LIT-1274](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1274.md), read in full in [NOTE-1002](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1002.md), with Lenggenhager et al. (2007), [LIT-1279](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1279.md), read in full in [NOTE-999](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-999.md), for the full-body illusion it leans on. Minimal phenomenal selfhood is given three dimensions: global self-identification, self-location and a weak first-person perspective. Out-of-body experience, heautoscopy and full-body illusions vary them; the rubber hand illusion is said not to. The necessity and sufficiency claims are asserted, and the agency thesis rests on adults whose agency was intact. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-769](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-769.md) v2 | Ownership of a body part is a graded belief that it is the most probable common cause of correlated multisensory input, so that synchronous stimulation of another object moves some of that belief to the object and away from the real part | Apps & Tsakiris (2014), [LIT-1262](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1262.md), read in full in [NOTE-991](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-991.md), with Botvinick & Cohen (1998), [LIT-1277](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1277.md), for the illusion it explains. The rubber hand, enfacement and rubber-voice illusions are read as one inference: unimodal surprise from synchronous stimulation is explained away by shifting the probability that a part is "me". The account fits the findings; its authors grant there is little direct evidence and that it is hard to falsify with standard fMRI. It does not say why such a model is experienced as a self. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-827](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-827.md) | The rubber hand illusion is a perceptual illusion driven by multisensory integration: the difference in reports between synchronous and asynchronous brushing is produced by the stimulation, not by participants' expectations | Ehrsson et al. (2022), [LIT-1264](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1264.md), read in [NOTE-997](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-997.md), conclude that the rubber hand illusion is a perceptual illusion driven primarily by multisensory mechanisms ([NOTE-997](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-997.md), C8), from the synchrony difference's independence of hypnotisability in Lush et al.'s 353 participants. Lush and Seth's reply, [LIT-1267](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1267.md), shows that uniform but unequal expectations predict the same null. | [THEORY-872](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-872.md) | A self-model compresses the sensory effects of a system's own activity by positing one stable common cause, at fast and slow timescales; there is such a pattern in the signal, so the self is real as a pattern and unreal as a substance, and realists and anti-realists about selves who accept this agree on the facts and differ on the criterion of reality | Gładziejewski (2025), [LIT-1360](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1360.md), read in full in [NOTE-1056](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1056.md), §4.1, after Hohwy & Michael (2017) and Letheby & Gerrans (2017), neither of which the record holds. An interpretation, not a result. The paper calls its self section "an initial sketch". It does not say that the self-model exaggerates the self's unity, though the exchange that filed the work said so. It says the single common cause is a compression, and that the verdict on selves turns on criteria. Its one candidate for a self-model that misdescribes is a dissociative case better compressed by two narrative selves. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1114](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1114.md) v2 | Which self-category a person uses, what it means and who in it is most typical vary lawfully with the comparative frame of reference: a grouping of self with others becomes salient as the differences within it shrink relative to the differences between it and the rest of the frame (metacontrast) and as those differences match expectations about the category, and as it does, self-perception is depersonalized | Self-categorization theory as restated by Turner, Oakes, Haslam and McGarty (1994), [LIT-1794](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1794.md), and reviewed by Hornsey (2008), [LIT-1742](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1742.md). Personal and social identity are levels of self-categorization. Salience is perceiver readiness times fit, comparative fit being the metacontrast ratio. The level, kind, content and prototype structure of self-categories shift with the comparison set: Americans read as less aggressive beside Iraq than beside the Soviet Union, and a group's extreme members become more prototypical in an intergroup context. Proposed: every result in the record comes through the theory's authors, reported without data, and the account's stronger claim, that the self is generated rather than stored, is not part of it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1115](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1115.md) | A we-identity, being one of us, can arise through mutual individualization, in which members grasp one another as non-substitutable and complementary, without depersonalization, as in long friendships and romantic partnerships; so depersonalization is not necessary for a we-identity | León (2023), [LIT-1721](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1721.md). Self-categorization theory claims depersonalization as "the basic process underlying group phenomena", for groups of any size, friendship groups included (Turner et al. 1987, pp. 50, 103, as quoted), and phenomenologists have taken it as the account of the "we". But close relationships yield we-identities while their members grasp each other as non-substitutable, and relationship research on couple resilience finds the "we" more adaptive the more differentiated the "I". Proposed: the argument is conceptual, and the cited evidence was not analysed by the source or read here. | Proposed |
